newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian stocks seen trading cautiously.
newsitem.headline: Asian stocks seen trading cautiously.

text.p: The outlook for Asian stocks this week was for cautious, range-bound trading, although investors could gain from bargain-hunting and companies with strong first-quarter earnings, analysts said.
A cloud over Asian markets lifted with a rally on Wall Street on Friday that reversed a downward trend. The Dow Jones Industrial average ended up 49 points, or 0.75 percent, at 6526.

U.S. stocks had suffered the fourth-largest point loss in New York Stock Exchange history last week. Analysts cautioned, however, that despite Friday's rally, the U.S. sell-off may not have run its course. - - - -
TOKYO - The Tokyo stock market's key index is likely to drift in a limited range this coming week, brokers said.

Shares in banks and property-related firms are expected to stay under selling pressure amid lingering worries about their bad loan problems. Securities houses are also seen vulnerable to further developments in the Nomura Securities scandal.
But blue-chip shares in the high-tech and electrical sectors are expected to extend gains, backed by strong earnings prospects, they said.
On Friday, the market's benchmark 225-share Nikkei average closed at 17,860.59, down 329.13 points or 1.8 percent from March 28.
Many brokers expected the Nikkei average to hover between 17,500 and 18,500 this week. - - - -

HONG KONG - The recent downtrend in share prices is expected to prompt cautious trading in the week ahead and although stocks could attempt a rebound, prices are likely to be confined to ranges, analysts said.
The Hang Seng Index shed 329.73 points, or 2.63 percent, last week to close at 12,204.59 on Friday.
Analysts said investors had been discounting a possible rise in U.S. interest rates in May and the impact of U.S. March jobs data, which showed ongoing economic strength, should be small.

"I would not be surprised to see more consolidation, to see the market testing 12,000 again just because there really is not that much to look forward to," said Kent Rossiter, institutional sales manager at Nikko Securities. - - - -

BANGKOK - Thai stocks are expected to gain slightly in the coming week on buying of discounted, blue-chip stocks but turnover will remain thin as the market still lacks positive news to boost investment, brokers said.
The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index advanced 0.71 percent in the week to 714.09 points on Friday from a week ago. It rose 1.14 percent from Thursday.

"The SET is expected to be sluggish next week as it operates only four days while investors are also awaiting first quarter earnings results. Local investors are expected to stay on the sidelines," said Chetta Meemangkang of Prime Finance and Securities.
The market will be closed on Monday for a public holiday.
Brokers said investors were also awaiting the entry of government pension and provident funds into the money market. - - - -
BOMBAY - Indian share prices are seen range-bound this week as players seek direction from a week-old political crisis, dealers said.

"I don't see anyone building positions ahead of the trust vote," Purvesh Shah, chief dealer at Nucleus Securities said. Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda faces a parliamentary test on April 11 after his key ally pulled its support on Sunday. The Bombay exchange index recovered partially on hopes a pro-market budget will survive the crisis.
The index fell over eight percent on Monday, but at week's close it was down 3.08 percent, or 113.16 points, at 3,550.37. - - - -
DHAKA - Dhaka stocks were jittery this past week after a court issued arrest orders for 36 brokers and company owners in connection with an inquiry into allegedly fraudulent acts.

But analysts were hopeful the market will soon recover from the initial shock, saying investors in general welcomed the crackdown on manipulation of share prices responsible for unusual ups and downs in the market late last year.
The Dhaka Stock Exchange benchmark index lost 19.12 points at 1,138.46 in the trading week which ended on Thursday. - - - -
JAKARTA - Bargain-hunting in selected big-caps should help keep the Jakarta stock index steady despite likely weak sentiment, brokers said.
"After a series of recent sharp falls, the overall tone is likely to stay weak, but we expect bargain-hunting to prevent any possible sharp falls and keep the index at least flat," one broker said.
Bimantara, cigarette maker Sampoerna and Tambang Timah were the big-capitalised stocks likely to be the targets of bargain-hunting, brokers said.
On Friday, the Jakarta composite index closed 4.19 points lower at 637.43 points against last week's close of 662.24 points.
KUALA LUMPUR - Sentiment has been battered as analysts digested the impact of the recent central bank annual report, which outlined plans to curb financing for property and share purchases.
Thursday and Friday were characterised by increasing calls by broking houses to leveraged clients to top up their portolios with cash.
Banking and property stocks were the hardest hit. Analysts said these sectors would take the brunt of the measures.

"If you bought on the rebound today, next week you should clear those holdings first and take profits. It was no more than a technical rebound," said Lynn Cheah Lee Ling, assistant manager at BHLB Asset Management in Kuala Lumpur.
"The long-term view for the Malaysian market is still positive, but in the short term we are negative," said Fiona Leong, head of research at J.M. Sassoon in Kuala Lumpur.
For the week the benchmark Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks closed 80.86 points, or 6.6 percent, lower to 1,136.78 from 1,217.64 on March 28. - - - -

MANILA - Philippine shares are likely to retrench, following the Dow's movements, traders said. "It seems the market has not reached its bottom. We don't expect any positive news to spur the market. Any technical rebound will probably be shortlived," said Elline Salvatierra of Dharmala Securities Phils Inc.

DBS Securities research head Francisco Trinidad said first quarter corporate results, generally expected to be strong, could be the source of any rally. The market's eagerly awaited rebound after the Easter holidays failed to materialise last week as the market took cues from a battered Dow.
The main index closed lower on Friday by 44.18 points, or 1.42 percent, to 3,060.59. Week-on-week, the index fell 162.55 points, or by 5.04 percent, from 3,223.14.
SEOUL - The market for South Korean stocks is expected to remain firmer in the belief the slowing economy has bottomed out, brokers said. Stable liquidity will also help improve investor sentiment.
The brokers said the index could rise to 720 during the week, a level many brokers see as a strong resistance.

"Much of the market's fall early this year was due to non-economic factors," said Kim Young-bum of Seoul Securities. "Now investors believe most of those factors had fizzled out and the market would pick up steadily."
The composite index closed at 687.42 on Friday, up 5.3 percent or 34.55 points from the previous Friday's 652.87.
SINGAPORE - Dealers said Wall Street's reaction to the U.S. March employment data late on Friday was expected to determine the market's direction.
"If it shows higher-than-expected growth, the markets are going to tumble and fears of rate hikes, which have been plaguing markets, are going to be be reinforced," said a dealer with a local house.
However, dealers said the downside was likely to be limited, with bargain-hunting likely to prop the Straits Times Industrials (STI) index around 2,035.00.

Jitters over Malaysian stocks following the central bank's curbs on bank loans for property and share purchases were likely to continue to weigh on sentiment, dealers said. The Malaysian news triggered a wave of forced selling brought on by margin calls on Thursday.
On Friday, the STI index ended at 2,075.78 against 2,098.92 the previous week.
